title: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market
oneLiner: Fewer landlords means fewer rentals, and fewer rentals means higher rents.
body: If the after-tax return on rental property falls, some investors will sell and fewer will buy. Opponents of reform argue that the resulting withdrawal of rental stock would raise rents for the tenants the policy is meant to help.
contextBackground: This was the central argument of the campaigns against reform in 2016 and 2019, and the main reason governments have not touched the concession since 1987.
contextDisagreement: Reform advocates answer that a home sold by an investor is usually bought by an owner-occupier who was renting, so the rental stock and the number of renters fall together. The empirical record from 1985–87 is read differently by each side.

otherClaim.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes

claimItself.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes
claimItself.oneLiner: The policy is now a bill before the Senate: negative gearing for new builds only from July 2027, existing investors grandfathered, and a reworked capital gains discount alongside it.
claimItself.body: The 12 May 2026 budget restricted negative gearing to newly built residential property for investments made after budget night, with effect from 1 July 2027, and replaced the 50 per cent capital gains discount with an inflation-based discount and a 30 per cent floor. Anyone using the concessions before budget night keeps them. A Senate inquiry took evidence in June 2026.

otherClaim.title: Modelling commissioned by the property industry forecasts rents about $9 a week higher and roughly 8,700 fewer homes by 2030 under the changes

claimItself.title: Modelling commissioned by the property industry forecasts rents about $9 a week higher and roughly 8,700 fewer homes by 2030 under the changes
claimItself.oneLiner: The competing estimate, from the groups opposing the bill.
claimItself.body: Qaive and Tulipwood Economics, commissioned by Master Builders Australia, the Property Council and the Real Estate Institute, forecast rents about $9 a week higher once the changes take effect, several times Treasury's figure, and about 8,700 fewer dwellings by 2029–30. The same modelling credits the budget's supply measures with far fewer homes than Treasury does.

otherClaim.title: Private landlords supply the large majority of Australia's rental housing

claimItself.title: Private landlords supply the large majority of Australia's rental housing
claimItself.oneLiner: Social and institutional housing is a small share; most renters rent from an individual.
claimItself.body: Census tenure data shows that most rented dwellings are owned by private individuals rather than by governments, community housing providers or institutional investors. Any policy that changes individual investors' behaviour therefore acts on most of the rental stock.

claimItself.title: Treasury estimates the 2026 changes would raise rents by less than $2 a week for a household on the median rent
claimItself.oneLiner: The official estimate of the rent effect is small.
claimItself.body: Treasury's budget modelling puts the rent effect of restricting negative gearing and reworking the capital gains discount at under $2 a week at the median, and estimates about 35,000 fewer homes over a decade, more than offset in its view by the budget's supply measures. Its secretary told the Senate the measures mainly shift ownership from investors to owner-occupiers.

otherClaim.title: When negative gearing was quarantined in 1985–87, rents rose sharply in Sydney and Perth but not in other capitals

claimItself.title: When negative gearing was quarantined in 1985–87, rents rose sharply in Sydney and Perth but not in other capitals
claimItself.oneLiner: The one time Australia tried this, the rent effect showed up in two cities with tight vacancy and nowhere else.
claimItself.body: Real rents rose strongly in Sydney and Perth during the quarantine period, which is the episode usually cited as proof that rents would spike. Rents in Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide were flat or fell in real terms over the same period, which suggests local vacancy rates, not the tax change, drove the increases.
